metadata.file_name: 23. Encarnação et al. (2025). Hierarchical clustering of the pre- exam anxiety levels in physically inactive and active adolescent students from 56 countries: an observational study using PISA program data.pdf
metadata.title: Hierarchical clustering of the pre-exam anxiety levels in physically inactive and active adolescent students from 56 countries: an observational study using PISA program data
metadata.venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 data (56 countries) but does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures in the clustering workflow. The authors state they did not have access to the raw dataset and instead relied on OECD-published chi-square outputs and country-level mean percentage anxiety values, which implies the analysis is conducted on aggregated country summaries rather than student-level weighted estimates. Because hierarchical clustering is applied to country-level anxiety percentages (and not to PV-based achievement scores), the manuscript does not specify any complex-survey variance estimation or weight variable usage. As a result, readers should treat the clustering outputs as descriptive patterns across countries rather than population-representative inference unless the authors’ weighting approach is clarified.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is country-level pre-exam anxiety percentages by physical activity status (low vs high), derived from PISA 2018 rather than modeled using PV-based cognitive achievement scores. The manuscript does not describe any missing-data strategy for the underlying student responses used to compute these country percentages, representing a reporting gap for transparency. Because the analysis is performed on aggregated country means and the authors do not provide the raw-data processing steps, the missing-data handling cannot be verified from the text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 country-level pre-exam anxiety percentages for 15-year-old students, restricted to countries with available anxiety and physical activity classification. Students were grouped into two physical activity statuses using PISA’s operational definition: low physical activity (no regular physical activity) vs high physical activity (moderate to vigorous regular physical activity). The clustering was performed separately for each physical activity group using country-level mean anxiety percentages; the authors also note that PISA included anxiety and physical activity only for students who reported feeling well-prepared for their exams, to reduce confounding from academic preparation.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) pre-exam anxiety by physical activity status — low physical activity group (country-level means)
main_findings.target_variable: Pre-exam anxiety percentage (low physical activity students)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical clustering (Euclidean distance; dendrogram cut at 20% y-axis). Best silhouette score: 0.60 (5 clusters). WCSS: 309.27; average square distance: 5.52; percentual average square distance: 2.35%. BCSS: 1,367.33; 96% variability explained; BCSS/WCSS ratio: 22.10.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 the study applied hierarchical clustering to country-level pre-exam anxiety percentages for students with low physical activity, finding two high-anxiety clusters (H-1: 67%, H-2: 78%) and three lower-anxiety clusters (L-1: 41%, L-2: 52%, L-3: 60%), with Brazil and the Dominican Republic among the most anxious countries. This indicates that countries can be grouped into distinct anxiety-risk profiles among physically inactive adolescents, suggesting that mental-health and physical-activity promotion policies should be prioritized and tailored to the most anxious country clusters rather than applied uniformly.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) pre-exam anxiety by physical activity status — high physical activity group (country-level means)
main_findings.target_variable: Pre-exam anxiety percentage (high physical activity students)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical clustering (Euclidean distance; dendrogram cut at 20% y-axis). Best silhouette score: 0.56 (4 clusters). WCSS: 632.80; average square distance: 5.52; percentual average square distance: 11.3%. BCSS: 7,079.18; 92% variability explained; BCSS/WCSS ratio: 11.18.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 the study applied hierarchical clustering to country-level pre-exam anxiety percentages for students with high physical activity, finding two low-anxiety clusters (L-1: 53%, L-2: 43%) and two higher-anxiety clusters (H-1: 77%, H-2: 64%), with Malaysia, Brazil, and Costa Rica among the most anxious. This indicates that physical activity does not uniformly eliminate pre-exam anxiety across countries, implying that country-specific academic-stress contexts and support systems should be integrated with physical-activity interventions.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) pre-exam anxiety by physical activity status — cross-group country differences
main_findings.target_variable: Difference in pre-exam anxiety percentage between low vs high physical activity groups
main_findings.performance_metrics: Country-level chi-square comparisons using a 95% CI threshold (Z ≥ 1.96). Statistically significant reductions (p < 0.05) for many countries (e.g., Austria −7, Belgium −8, Chile −8, France −5, Germany −2, Greece −7, Hungary −7, Israel −9, Korea −5, Mexico −7, Turkey −5, United States −9). Exceptions: Russia +11% and United Arab Emirates +4%. Overall mean change across countries: −3% (p < 0.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 the study compared country-level pre-exam anxiety percentages between low and high physical activity groups and found an overall average reduction of −3% (p < 0.01), with most countries showing statistically significant decreases. This indicates that promoting regular moderate-to-vigorous physical activity may reduce pre-exam anxiety for many adolescents, but the presence of exceptions (e.g., Russia and the UAE) suggests that interventions must account for local academic and cultural stressors, and causality cannot be inferred from this observational clustering approach.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 country-level pre-exam anxiety percentages for 15-year-old students, stratified by physical activity status (low/no regular activity vs high/moderate-vigorous regular activity). It performs hierarchical clustering using Euclidean distance and selects the number of clusters via dendrogram cut at 20% plus silhouette score and dispersion metrics. For low physical activity students, the best solution used 5 clusters with silhouette = 0.60, WCSS = 309.27, 96% variability explained (BCSS), and BCSS/WCSS = 22.10; Brazil (82%) and the Dominican Republic (81%) were among the most anxious. For high physical activity students, the best solution used 4 clusters with silhouette = 0.56, WCSS = 632.80, 92% variability explained, and BCSS/WCSS = 11.18; Malaysia (82%), Brazil (81%), and Costa Rica (81%) were most anxious. Across countries, the average anxiety difference between low vs high physical activity was −3% (p < 0.01), with Russia (+11%) and the UAE (+4%) as exceptions. Limitations include reliance on aggregated country means (no student-level PV modeling), lack of reported missing-data handling, and no explicit survey-weighted inference.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper is an observational clustering study using hierarchical clustering on country-level anxiety percentages rather than a supervised predictive ML model. As a result, no predictive algorithm is evaluated for accuracy/AUC/RMSE, and the schema’s ML technique fields are left empty (primary = null, all_techniques = []). The study still reports clustering quality metrics (silhouette, WCSS/BCSS), which are appropriate for exploratory clustering but do not map to the schema’s predictive-model algorithm list.
